source.title_on_document: The role of task breadth and cognitive flexibility in generative AI-supported creative idea generation

supplement.where: The paper refers to no online supplement. Appendices A to E are printed in this PDF (pp. 13-19).
supplement.holds: Nothing outside this PDF. Appendix D (p. 18) holds the expert ratings of novelty, usefulness, and creativity and the number of ideas, as arm means, SDs, and Ns only.

paper_design_summary: Two online between-subjects experiments on new-venture idea generation. Participants were randomly assigned to see startup ideas generated by a fine-tuned GPT-3 model as optional inspiration (10 ideas in Study 1, a broad task; 4 ideas in Study 2, a narrow EdTech task) or to see no AI ideas. The primary outcome is breadth of exploration (number of hand-coded semantic categories in each participant's ideas); the paper also reports depth of exploration, cosine similarity of ideas across participants, and, in Appendix D, expert ratings of novelty, usefulness, and creativity and the number of ideas.

studies.label: Study 1 (broad startup idea task, master's students)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Exposure to 10 randomly drawn LLM-generated startup ideas as optional inspiration versus no AI ideas
assignment.quote: Ninety-three participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: exposed to ideas generated by a fine-tuned LLM ( n = 46) or no exposure to LLM-generated ideas ( n = 47).

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Saw 10 ideas randomly extracted from a database of 453 ideas from a fine-tuned GPT-3 startup-idea generator, with no obligation to use them; told the ideas came from artificial intelligence and not to suggest an identical idea

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same scenario and instructions, no AI ideas shown

participants.exclusions: Three participants excluded because they failed to complete the experiment (p. 6). Table 4 gives N = 45 per arm (p. 9), so one LLM-arm and two human-only participants were dropped.
participants.who: International master's students in management who had taken at least one entrepreneurship course; mean age about 23; 65 percent female
participants.country: not_stated (91 percent took the study in French, 9 percent in English; authors at SKEMA Business School and Universite Cote d'Azur, France)
participants.quote: All participants were international master's students specializing in the field of management who attended at least one course related to entrepreneurship.

ai_tool.name_model: Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI (2022), a GPT-3 model fine-tuned on descriptions of seed-funded startups with prompt-based human feedback (Appendix A)
ai_tool.how_used: Ten pre-generated ideas, drawn at random from 453 screened ideas, displayed on the idea-entry page as optional inspiration; participants could not interact with the model. Study ran before the release of ChatGPT (pp. 6-7).

task.description: Suggest startup ideas for an incubator call (business need, product or service, revenue source, target customer); any domain allowed (broad task)
task.duration: Minimum 8 min, instructed to spend about 10 min, no maximum (p. 8, Section 4.5)

outcomes.name: Breadth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories (out of 15 inductively derived categories) spanned by a participant's ideas; one author built the scheme, an independent researcher assigned each idea; 99 percent agreement within 1 point, ICC 0.97; scores averaged across raters (p. 7, Section 4.4.1; Appendix C). Kruskal-Wallis test because of non-normality (Appendix E); paper says parametric tests give similar conclusions.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 2.32 (SD 1.32, N 45) vs Human-only 1.60 (SD 0.74, N 45); d = 0.67. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 6.43, p = 0.01; significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction for the two primary outcome tests.

outcomes.name: Depth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas divided by breadth of exploration (ideas per explored category), a measure of cognitive persistence (p. 8, Section 4.4.2). No hypothesis was stated for it, but the paper counts it as one of the two primary outcome tests.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 1.13 (SD 0.26, N 45) vs Human-only 1.15 (SD 0.33, N 45); d = 0.07. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.45, p = 0.50.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity among ideas within condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise cosine similarity of SpaCy sentence embeddings after tokenization, stop-word and common-word removal, lemmatization; first idea of each participant only. Paper labels it exploratory, not a hypothesis test (p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity Human-only M = 0.81 (SD 0.08) vs LLM-assisted M = 0.74 (SD 0.13); M difference = 0.07, 95% CI [0.04, 0.10], p = 0.00, Cohen's d = 0.91 (permutation test, 10,000 iterations). Table 7: N (ideas) 45 per arm, permutation p = 0.00. Sign reversed: lower similarity in the LLM arm means more diversity. No SE is printed; the mean difference comes with a CI.

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity between ideas within a condition (higher = more homogeneous)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SpaCy package sentence embeddings (model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each condition, using only the first idea generated by each participant (45 ideas per arm)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 10,000 iterations; 95% CI on the mean difference
diversity_detail.notes: Paper reports similarity; sign reversed for the atlas (treatment more diverse). The same section compares human-only ideas with the pool of LLM-generated stimuli (M difference = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.12, -0.09], p = 0.00, d = -1.74), an AI-versus-human output comparison not listed as an outcome.

outcomes.name: Average creativity (expert rating, mean of novelty and usefulness)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique; each idea rated by at least two of six expert judges (entrepreneurship program heads, accelerator jury member, consultant, serial entrepreneur) on 7-point scales; creativity = mean of novelty and usefulness; idea-level scores averaged to participant level; 84.6 percent agreement within 1.5 points. Descriptive and exploratory, not used to test the hypothesis (Appendix D).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.23 (0.37, 45) vs Human-only 4.35 (0.44, 45), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported. Appendix D text: breadth gain 'did not translate into higher novelty or creativity ratings'.
contrasts.locator: p. 18, Appendix D, Descriptive statistics; p. 19, Interpretation

outcomes.name: Average novelty (expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three items (newness, uniqueness, unusualness), 7-point scales, at least two expert judges per idea, averaged to participant level; 68.4 percent agreement within 1.5 points (Appendix D).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 3.90 (0.79, 45) vs Human-only 3.97 (0.72, 45), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported.

outcomes.name: Average usefulness (expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Feasibility and operability items (a third item was dropped after Study 1 for low internal consistency), 7-point scales, at least two expert judges per idea, averaged to participant level; 65.5 percent agreement within 1.5 points (Appendix D).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.57 (0.54, 45) vs Human-only 4.73 (0.69, 45), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas generated per participant (Appendix D). Total 208 ideas, 2.3 per participant (p. 8, Section 4.6).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 2.71 (1.90, 45) vs Human-only 1.91 (1.40, 45), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported.

studies.label: Study 2 (narrow EdTech startup idea task, Prolific UK entrepreneurs)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Exposure to 4 randomly drawn LLM-generated education startup ideas as optional inspiration versus no AI ideas
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: use of LLM-generated ideas ( n = 60) versus no use ( n = 60).

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Saw four ideas drawn at random (different for each participant) from 44 education-related ideas from the same fine-tuned GPT-3 model, labeled as generated by an AI system, 'Be free to ignore if not useful'

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same scenario and instructions, no AI ideas shown

participants.exclusions: Five ideas and three participants excluded for unrelatedness to the task; the paper says including them leaves breadth and depth results qualitatively unchanged (p. 9). Analyzed: 59 LLM-assisted, 58 human-only (p. 9, Section 5.5; Table 6).
participants.who: Prolific Academic UK panel members, pre-screened on approval rate and English proficiency, all self-declared current engagement in entrepreneurship or owning a business; mean age about 43; 51 percent female
participants.country: United Kingdom (Prolific UK panel; more than 90 percent born in the UK)
participants.quote: Participants were members of the Prolific Academic United Kingdom online research panel.

ai_tool.name_model: Same fine-tuned GPT-3 startup-idea model as Study 1 (Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI)
ai_tool.how_used: Four pre-generated education-related ideas displayed as optional inspiration; no interaction with the model. Study ran before the public release of generative AI models (p. 9, Section 5.2).

task.description: Suggest startup ideas related to the use of technology in education (need, target customer, technological solution, revenue source); narrow task
task.duration: Minimum 8 min, instructed to spend about 10 min; complete participation about 11 min (p. 9, Section 5.4)

outcomes.name: Breadth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories (out of 11 categories, Appendix C) spanned by a participant's ideas; one author categorized, an external researcher independently checked (p. 9, Section 5.4). Kruskal-Wallis test; paper says a parametric test gives the same conclusions.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 1.39 (SD 0.70, N 59) vs Human-only 1.38 (SD 0.67, N 58); d = 0.01. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.00, p = 1.00.

outcomes.name: Depth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas divided by breadth of exploration (cognitive persistence); one of the two primary analyses (p. 10, Section 5.5.1).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 1.16 (SD 0.48, N 59) vs Human-only 1.11 (SD 0.35, N 58); d = 0.12. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.07, p = 0.79.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity among ideas within condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise cosine similarity, computed 'parallel to' Study 1 (SpaCy embeddings, first idea per participant as in Study 1; Table 7 lists N (ideas) 59 and 58). Exploratory (p. 10, Section 5.5.2).

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity Human-only M = 0.87 (SD 0.04) vs LLM-assisted M = 0.87 (SD 0.05); M difference = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.02], p = 0.09, Cohen's d = 0.31 (permutation test, 10,000 iterations). Table 7: N (ideas) 59 LLM-assisted, 58 human-only, permutation p = 0.09. No SE printed.

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity between ideas within a condition (higher = more homogeneous)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SpaCy package sentence embeddings, by reference to Study 1 (model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each condition; Table 7 N (ideas) = 59 and 58, consistent with one idea per participant as in Study 1
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 10,000 iterations; 95% CI on the mean difference
diversity_detail.notes: Paper reports similarity; sign reversed for the atlas. Whether only first ideas were used in Study 2 is implied by 'parallel to those in Study 1' and Table 7 Ns, not stated outright. The pool of LLM stimuli had M = 0.77 (SD 0.10), an AI-versus-human comparison not listed as an outcome.

outcomes.name: Average creativity (expert rating, mean of novelty and usefulness)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two expert judges (entrepreneurship department director; management researcher trained in entrepreneurship) rated all 183 ideas on 7-point scales; initial usefulness agreement was insufficient, so judges discussed discrepancies before final aggregation; idea-level scores averaged to participant level. Descriptive and exploratory (Appendix D).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.86 (0.74, 59) vs Human-only 4.52 (0.88, 58), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported.

outcomes.name: Average novelty (expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three items (newness, uniqueness, unusualness), 7-point scales, two expert judges, averaged to participant level (Appendix D).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.61 (0.87, 59) vs Human-only 4.41 (0.91, 58), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported.

outcomes.name: Average usefulness (expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Feasibility and operability items, 7-point scales, two expert judges who reconciled discrepancies before aggregation, averaged to participant level (Appendix D).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 5.11 (1.04, 59) vs Human-only 4.60 (1.16, 58), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas generated per participant (Appendix D). Total 183 ideas, 1.56 per participant (p. 9, Section 5.5).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 1.61 (1.02, 59) vs Human-only 1.52 (0.78, 58), M (SD, N). Descriptive only; no test reported.

company_involvement.description: Authors declare no competing interests (p. 13). The stimulus tool is a third-party fine-tuned GPT-3 product (Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI); no company role in the study is stated.

data_and_code.data_url: Data will be made available on request (p. 19)

eligibility.reason: Both studies randomly assign individuals to see LLM-generated startup ideas or no AI ideas (pp. 6, 9). Study 1 analyzes 90 of 93 randomized people, Study 2 analyzes 117 of 120. Outcomes are scored on participants' ideas: hand-coded category breadth (flexibility), embedding similarity across participants, and expert ratings of novelty, usefulness, and creativity (Appendix D, descriptive only). The AI role is pre-generated ideas from a fine-tuned GPT-3 shown as stimuli, with no interaction.

one_line_finding: Seeing 10 fine-tuned-GPT-3 startup ideas raised breadth of exploration in a broad task (2.32 vs 1.60 categories, d = 0.67, Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.01; Study 1, p. 9, Table 4) and lowered cross-participant similarity (0.74 vs 0.81), but had no effect in a narrow EdTech task (1.39 vs 1.38, p = 1.00; Study 2, p. 11, Table 6); expert creativity ratings show no gain in Study 1 (4.23 vs 4.35, Appendix D).
open_questions: Study 1 recruited master's students by cold email and ran unsupervised online; online_rct is the closest code, though it is not a panel.
Study 2 exclusions are by 'unrelatedness to the task', applied after assignment; the per-arm split (1 vs 2) is inferred from Table 6 Ns.

Expert ratings (Appendix D) have no tests or SEs; only arm means, SDs, and Ns. Under the codebook's primary-record rule, overall creativity rated by people would outrank breadth for with_ai, but the paper names breadth as primary.
Studies differ in both task breadth and number of stimuli (10 vs 4); the paper notes it cannot rule out a dose effect (p. 13).
notes: Two experiments, each with one AI arm and one no-AI arm. The control arm in Study 1 was told it could do some internet research, as was the AI arm (Appendix B). Similarity analyses also compare human-only ideas with the pool of LLM stimuli (Study 1: M difference -0.10, 95% CI [-0.12, -0.09], p = 0.00, d = -1.74; Study 2 stimulus pool M = 0.77, SD 0.10); these are AI-versus-human comparisons, recorded here and not as outcomes. A manipulation check found 78 percent (Study 1) and 92 percent (Study 2) recognized the ideas as AI-generated; dropping those who did not leaves results unchanged (pp. 7, 9). Not preregistered as far as the paper states; a priori power analysis targeted 76 participants per study.
